genZNote: Start it on a cephalosporin and watch it develop resistance mid-treatment — the AmpC gene doesn't play fair.

habitat.naturalHabitat: Human and animal GI tract; widely distributed in soil, water, and sewage
habitat.hostAssociation: Normal gut flora in some individuals; opportunistic nosocomial pathogen
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Common in soil, water, and plant surfaces
habitat.reservoir: Human GI tract and hospital environment (equipment, hands)

culture.colonyMorphology: Large, mucoid, pink colonies (lactose fermenter, often slow/variable)

identificationClues: Gram-negative motile rod, variable/slow lactose fermentation on MacConkey
Can induce chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase during cephalosporin therapy, leading to resistance emerging mid-treatment
A classic member of the 'SPICE' organisms (Serratia, Pseudomonas/Proteus, Indole-positive Proteus, Citrobacter, Enterobacter) with inducible AmpC

diseases: Bacteremia, especially in critically ill or catheterized patients
virulenceFactors: Inducible chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase — confers resistance to many cephalosporins, sometimes emerging during treatment
clinicalImportance.transmission: Endogenous flora or healthcare-associated transmission via contaminated equipment/hands
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: An important cause of nosocomial infections, particularly in intensive care settings; notable for the risk of resistance developing during third-generation cephalosporin therapy due to AmpC derepression
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Clinicians should be cautious using third-generation cephalosporins alone for serious Enterobacter infections due to the risk of AmpC-mediated resistance emerging during treatment

examFacts.importantTest: Susceptibility testing to monitor for inducible AmpC resistance during cephalosporin therapy
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Inducible chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase that can cause resistance to emerge mid-treatment on third-generation cephalosporins
